The ACC's 2026-06-30 release on the Second Universal Definition of Heart Failure says the next AHA/ACC management guideline is expected in late 2027, so the 2022 guideline is still current. brief.situation: 04:50 on a medical unit. Mrs. Bennett in Room 22, 76, admitted yesterday at 05:00 with pneumonia, puts her call light on: "I can't breathe lying down." She is on telemetry and continuous pulse oximetry.
handover: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (EF 30%). Her home furosemide 40 mg by mouth daily was held on admission because she looked dry.
0.9% saline has run at 100 mL/h since admission. Ceftriaxone and azithromycin for the pneumonia. Oxygen 2 L by nasal cannula, SpO2 94% at midnight.
Night orders: notify the provider for SpO2 below 90%; daily weight at 05:00. This morning's 04:00 labs are back.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Recognize what this is, act, escalate, and check that the treatment is working. Orders and the drug's effect take a few minutes.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. The case ends by 07:00, then a debrief scores what you did.

cues.question: What findings tell you this is heart failure and not the pneumonia, why tonight, and what makes it an emergency?

parts.label: Findings and why tonight
parts.criteria: Names orthopnea, crackles, distended neck veins, graded pitting edema, a 1.8 kg weight gain and a positive fluid balance with low oxygen and fast breathing as fluid overload in a heart with an EF of 30%; links it to 24 hours of saline with her furosemide held; ranks it above worsening pneumonia.
parts.modelAnswer: She can't lie flat, has crackles to mid-lung, distended neck veins and 2+ ankle edema, is up 1.8 kg and 1.75 L positive, with SpO2 88% and RR 27. In someone with an EF of 30% who has had 2.4 L of saline and no furosemide, that is acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary edema, not the pneumonia getting worse.

parts.label: Why it's an emergency and what to do
parts.criteria: Treats pulmonary edema as an emergency: sits her up, raises the oxygen to keep SpO2 at least 90%, stops the saline, calls the provider with an SBAR asking for IV furosemide, gives it promptly, checks potassium, measures urine output to judge the response, and escalates to the rapid response team for BiPAP if she stays in distress; no fluid bolus or sedative.
parts.modelAnswer: Fluid in the alveoli can tire her into respiratory failure, so: upright, more oxygen to keep SpO2 at least 90%, stop the saline, SBAR to the provider asking for IV furosemide, give it as soon as it's ordered after checking her potassium, then measure urine output: more than 100-150 mL an hour means it's working. If she stays below 90% or above 25 breaths a minute, the rapid response team for BiPAP. No bolus, no lorazepam.

noProgress.rationale: Still in pulmonary edema two hours after the first call light means two hours of hypoxemia in a heart that cannot cope; this case calls it harm.

expertPath.text: Look and listen: orthopnea, crackles to mid-lung, distended neck veins, 2+ ankle edema. Sit her up, oxygen up, stop the saline.
Weight +1.8 kg, intake/output +1,750 mL, potassium 3.6. SBAR to the provider: pulmonary edema from fluid overload; IV furosemide please.
Orders in: furosemide 40 mg IV at once. Objective note.
Urine output measured (well over 100-150 mL an hour); SpO2 above 92%, RR falling.

intubated.headline: Respiratory failure
intubated.body: Orthopnea, crackles and distended neck veins after a day of saline with her furosemide held is pulmonary edema. Find when she was sat up, when the saline stopped, and when furosemide went in.

decongesting.headline: Recognized and treated as an emergency
decongesting.body: Upright, oxygen, saline off, a clear SBAR, furosemide within minutes of the order, and urine output measured to prove it worked. That is the expert path.

decongestingLate.headline: Improving, by a slower route
decongestingLate.body: She is improving, but check how quickly she was sat up and given oxygen, when the saline stopped, whether the call named heart failure, whether BiPAP was needed, and whether the response was measured.

time_up.headline: Still in pulmonary edema at 07:00
time_up.body: Oxygen and position buy time; a diuretic removes the fluid. Without an SBAR that names fluid overload, the order never comes.

scoring.modelReasoning: Orthopnea, crackles to mid-lung, distended neck veins, 2+ pitting edema, a 1.8 kg gain and a 1.75 L positive balance in a client with an EF of 30%, after 24 hours of saline with her furosemide held, is acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary edema, not worsening pneumonia. It is an emergency: sit her upright with her legs down, raise the oxygen to keep SpO2 at least 90%, stop the saline, and call the provider with an SBAR that names fluid overload and asks for IV furosemide (the ESC starts at 1-2 times the daily oral dose). Check potassium, give the furosemide as soon as it is ordered (onset within 5 minutes, peak within 30), and evaluate by urine output: more than 100-150 mL an hour is a satisfactory response. If she stays below 90% or above 25 breaths a minute, the rapid response team for non-invasive ventilation. A fluid bolus or a sedative makes it worse.
